item.title: Variational Real-Time Dynamics on Reduced Operator Manifolds
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Operator-projected variational quantum real-time evolution (OVQRTE) updates parameterized circuits by matching Ehrenfest equations on polynomial-sized operator sets without quantum geometric tensor calculation. Reaches ground-state energy error ∼3×10−3 when generating QSCI subspaces on a 20-qubit simulator and executes on up to 24 superconducting qubits.

Grade 0.429 · 3.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Aeishah Ameera Anuar, PV Sriluckshmy, Riccardo Rossi, Fedor Simkovic

Figure

Energy error |E−EFCI| as a function of the cutoff fraction of the configuration interaction subspace size R, comparing exact time evolution to OVQRTE with SPSA gradient estimation across various evolution iterations for a 20-qubit system.

Asks

How can variational real-time dynamics be formulated to avoid measuring the quantum geometric tensor while reducing quantum circuit and measurement costs?

But

Demonstrated for systems up to 24 qubits, tested with Ns=22 SPSA samples per gradient step, requires selected reduced operator manifolds.

Tools

Operator-projected variational quantum real-time evolution (OVQRTE) · Simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation (SPSA) · Quantum-selected configuration interaction (QSCI) · Low-depth unitary coupled cluster Jastrow (LUCJ) ansatz · IQM Emerald superconducting processor

Abstract

Accurate real-time simulation of correlated quantum systems remains challenging for both classical methods and near-term quantum hardware. We introduce operator-projected variational quantum real-time evolution (OVQRTE), which updates a parameterized circuit by enforcing the Ehrenfest equations for a selected set of observables. OVQRTE requires only expectation-value measurements, while the choice of operator set enables a systematic trade-off between accuracy and measurement cost, substantially reducing quantum-resource requirements relative to existing variational real-time-evolution algorithms. After implementing OVQRTE dynamics of Heisenberg model on a simulator, we benchmark the algorithm for the Anderson impurity models on the IQM Emerald superconducting processor using up to 24 qubits. We further use OVQRTE to sample computational-basis states for quantum-selected configuration interaction (QSCI), enabling the calculation of the ground-state energy and density of states within a self-consistent ghost-Gutzwiller Ansatz (gGut) embedding loop. Our results establish OVQRTE as a promising approach for investigating correlated condensed-matter systems on near-term quantum hardware.

item.title: NAQsim: Full-Stack Architecture Simulation Framework for Fast and Space-Efficient Neutral Atom Quantum Computing
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Patch rotations cause 55.3% to 77.6% of execution time in transversal neutral-atom FTQC. The D3-ROT architecture eliminates this bottleneck, yielding an average 2.27× speedup (up to 2.57×) at 22.4% average footprint overhead.

Grade 0.400 · 2.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Yosuke Ueno, Shinichi Sunami, Toshihide Hinokuma, Yasunari Suzuki, Akihisa Goban, Hayata Yamasaki, Teruo Tanimoto, Ilkwon Byun

Figure

Per-layer latency breakdown (bars, left axis) and logical error rate (line, right axis) across six routing and patch-rotation architectures, showing D3-ROT minimizing latency without sacrificing error rates.

Asks

How can full-stack co-optimization across compiler, control hardware, and qubit plane reduce logical operation latency in transversal neutral-atom FTQC architectures?

Before

Patch rotations executed via space-efficient reflection on baseline transversal surface-code architectures.

But

Evaluated via classical CPU simulation across 8 FTQC benchmark circuits (QPE and FTCircuitBench) using rotated transversal surface codes.

Tools

NAQsim architecture simulation framework · SLM laser toggling with AOD atom holding · heterogeneous qubit-plane rotation patches · rotation distribution compiler pass

Code. https://github.com/naqsim/naqsim

Abstract

Technological advances in neutral-atom platforms have opened a new path toward designing efficient protocols for fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC). However, each physical operation is still orders of magnitude slower than on other platforms, such as superconducting qubits. Therefore, architects must identify fast and efficient FTQC architectures, which require reliable modeling tools to explore various design choices across the software, classical hardware, and quantum device stacks of neutral-atom platforms. In this paper, we propose NAQsim, an open-source simulation framework for neutral-atom FTQC architectures based on transversal gates. As its key feature, NAQsim enables detailed full-stack architecture evaluation that opens opportunities to explore previously overlooked performance bottlenecks. As a first use case for NAQsim, we identify one such bottleneck, patch rotations, perform full-stack co-optimization, and finally derive a near-rotation-free architecture (D3-ROT). For practical FTQC benchmark workloads, D3-ROT achieves a 2.27x speedup from this single bottleneck alone, with minimal footprint overhead. These results point to a much broader space of full-stack optimizations that NAQsim makes accessible for transversal surface-code architectures and beyond.

item.title: OpenQARP: a modular framework for quantum application research
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — OpenQARP executes operator algebra one to two orders of magnitude faster than OpenFermion and matches mature compilers on two-qubit gate count while keeping strict unified conventions.

Grade 0.396 · 2.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Theory of Trotter Error with Commutator Scaling” · Stefano Scali, Vicente P. Soloviev, Antonio Márquez Romero, Brian Coyle, Giuseppe Buonaiuto, Annie Paine, Jonathan H. Fetherolf, Marcos Diez García, Michal Krompiec, Josh Kirsopp

Figure

Run-phase simulation time on a logarithmic vertical axis plotted against register size for brickwork circuits, comparing constant-factor scaling across different quantum simulation frameworks.

Asks

How to build an open-source quantum computing framework that eliminates silent convention errors across the research workflow while maintaining high simulator and operator performance?

Before

OpenFermion, Qiskit/Aer, PennyLane/Lightning, Qulacs, qsim, and pytket required cross-framework plumbing with differing qubit orderings and phase conventions.

But

Benchmarks measured on a single Apple-silicon host using scalar C++ block kernels without SIMD or AVX vectorization; no pulse-level control, autodiff, or direct hardware execution engine.

Tools

C++20 compiled core with Python interface · block-based circuit abstraction · gate fusion and flip-mask Pauli contraction · independent NumPy/SciPy testing oracles

Code. https://github.com/OpenQARP/openqarp

Abstract

We introduce OpenQARP, the Open Quantum Application Research Package: an open-source Python framework for quantum application research, built on a compiled C++ core. In OpenQARP, an application is assembled from an algorithm library that orchestrates three interchangeable layers: blocks describe circuits, primitives describe what to extract from them, and engines describe how they run. The release spans near-term through fault-tolerant methods, targeting problems from electronic structure to combinatorial optimization, with device-aware compilation, circuit cutting, and resource estimation over a single set of numerical conventions that the code must follow. Every numerical feature is checked against an independent oracle, and every published timing carries a correctness check. Against OpenFermion, Qiskit/Aer, PennyLane/Lightning, Qulacs, qsim, and pytket, OpenQARP is one to two orders of magnitude faster on operator algebra and among the fastest on simulation. It matches mature compilers on two-qubit gate count, and expresses a complete algorithm in the lines a framework needs rather than the plumbing a primitive stack demands.

item.title: Open Quantum Systems
item.description:
Pay dirt review — Pedagogical review and lecture notes covering open quantum systems, microscopic derivations of GKSL master equations, Liouvillian spectral properties, and foundational quantum thermodynamics.

Grade 0.385 · 2.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “thermalization, many-body localization and quantum scars in driven systems” · Erik Torrontegui, Ricardo Puebla

Figure

Figure 1: Representation of a general qubit state ρ on the Bloch sphere. The relation between the position of the state on the ball and the density matrix ρ is established by the projections of the Bloch vector v→ on the Cartesian axis according to Eq. ( 44 ). Pure states |ψ⟩ ( |v→|=1 ) are located on the surface while the completely mixed state ρ_cm=mdmathbbI/2 ( |v→|=0 ) is placed at the origin.

Asks

How do environmental interactions generate decoherence, dissipation, and thermodynamic behavior in reduced quantum systems?

But

Primarily treats weak-coupling Markovian regimes via Born-Markov and secular approximations; omits non-Markovian dynamics, strong-coupling thermodynamics, and collision models.

Tools

density matrix formalism · GKSL master equation · Liouvillian superoperators · Born-Markov approximation · quantum data processing inequality

Abstract

Open quantum systems describe quantum systems that interact unavoidably with their environments. These notes introduce the physical origins of decoherence and dissipation in realistic settings, developing the theoretical framework of reduced dynamics and quantum master equations within the connection to thermodynamics in the quantum regime. Additionally, a set of relevant exercises are proposed to reinforce the acquisition of knowledge. The text equips readers with the tools to model and analyze open quantum dynamics.

item.title: A Modular, Topology-Aware Software Stack for Entanglement-Based Distributed Quantum Computing
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — For an 18-qubit QFT circuit on a 2-QPU network, replacing all-to-all with nearest-neighbor intra-QPU connectivity increases EPR-pair consumption by more than an order of magnitude. Under stochastic link generation, shortest-duration and critical-path arbitration policies reduce completion time by 17.7±1.3% and 17.9±1.5% relative to FIFO.

Grade 0.383 · 2.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Luke Andreesen, Shobhit Gupta, Sean Sullivan, Manish Kumar Singh

Figure

EPR-pair consumption (y-axis) for 18-qubit QFT and 64-qubit Adder circuits on a 2-QPU network under all-to-all versus nearest-neighbor intra-QPU connectivity (x-axis) across three partitioning strategies.

Asks

How can hardware network topology and link contention be incorporated into an open-source software stack for partitioning, compiling, and scheduling distributed quantum circuits?

Before

Prior distributed compilers (such as Pytket-DQC) lack timestamped operation scheduling and rely on idealized, optimistic all-to-all connectivity assumptions.

But

NISQ-era compilation only; does not model decoherence, noise, link fidelity degradation, entanglement distillation, or quantum error correction.

Tools

OpenQASM compiler toolchain · Discrete-event stochastic scheduler · Quantum Network Constructor (QNC) · Hypergraph and Dynamic Interaction circuit partitioners · Cat-Entangler and Cat-Disentangler teleportation protocols

Code. https://github.com/memQGit/dqc

Abstract

Distributed quantum computing (DQC) seeks to scale beyond the limits of monolithic processors by interconnecting multiple quantum processing units (QPUs) through entanglement-based links. Realizing this vision requires the co-design of hardware and software across the domains of quantum networking, compilation, and scheduling, yet existing tools remain fragmented between monolithic circuit compilers and long-distance quantum network simulators. We present an open-source, topology-informed framework for the compilation and scheduling of distributed quantum programs. Given an input circuit and a description of the target network, the framework partitions and reconstructs the circuit into a distributed program that respects the specified inter- and intra-QPU topology, covers cross-QPU operations through gate and state teleportation, and schedules the result under either deterministic or stochastic entanglement-generation models. By accepting and emitting standard OpenQASM, the framework interoperates with existing monolithic toolchains, and its standardized module interfaces allow partitioning and scheduling strategies to be interchanged and benchmarked. Using this framework, we show that the best-performing compilation strategy varies across the tested circuits and network configurations, and that both network topology and intra-QPU connectivity substantially affect the entanglement cost of execution. These findings underscore the need for a co-design approach to distributed quantum computing, which our framework is designed to support.

item.title: Exact quantum circuits for a Heisenberg triangle with Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Exact quantum circuits for three-spin Heisenberg-DM triangles require at most 8 CNOT gates for pure DM interactions, 10 CNOT gates for uniform exchange and DM couplings, and 14 CNOT gates for unequal couplings satisfying J2=D12D23+D23D31+D31D12.

Grade 0.377 · 2.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Andrey Zhukov

Figure

Exact circuit implementations of three-spin triangle evolution. Panel (a) uses 8 CNOT gates for pure DM interactions with arbitrary couplings, and panel (b) uses 10 CNOT gates for equal Heisenberg and DM couplings.

Asks

How can coupled time evolution on a three-spin Heisenberg triangle with Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interactions be compiled into exact, time-independent-depth quantum circuits across the full Hilbert space?

But

Unequal DM with exchange requires J2=D12D23+D23D31+D31D12. Valid on spin-1/2 systems without noise or decoherence.

Tools

unitary basis transformation · quaternion parameter matching · local z-rotations · symmetric Strang step analytical retuning

Abstract

We construct exact quantum circuits for a three-spin Heisenberg triangle with Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) interaction. A change of basis reduces pure DM evolution with arbitrary couplings to two single-qubit rotations, giving a circuit with at most 8 CNOT gates. When J and D are each the same on all bonds, one fixed basis gives a circuit with at most 10 CNOT gates for any real J,D,t. Local spin rotations extend the construction to a family with unequal DM couplings and nonzero exchange, requiring at most 14 CNOT gates. All circuits act on the full Hilbert space. An alternative pure DM implementation uses five two-qubit DM gates: analytically retuning the angles of one symmetric Strang step makes it exact. A 12-spin kagome example illustrates the use of these exact local blocks in lattice simulation.

item.title: Efficient expectation value estimation for quantum circuits via extended stabilizer frameworks and adaptive variance estimation
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Sample complexity dependence on gate-wise stabilizer extent drops from quadratic to linear in the low-variance regime via empirical variance-based confidence bounds instead of Hoeffding's inequality, maintaining prior space complexity.

Grade 0.363 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Practical quantum advantage in quantum simulation” · Yunseo Hwang, Giwon Song, Kyoung Keun Park, Hyukjoon Kwon, Taehyun Kim

Asks

Can classical expectation value estimation for non-Clifford quantum circuits be accelerated by combining sum-over-Clifford and quasi-probability methods with adaptive stopping criteria?

Before

Standard quasi-probability and sum-over-Clifford stabilizer simulators relied on Hoeffding's inequality, yielding quadratic sample-complexity overhead in the gate-wise stabilizer extent.

But

Sample complexity advantage holds in the low-variance regime. Validated on random circuits, T-doped Clifford circuits, QAOA, and quantum kernel models.

Tools

sum-over-Clifford simulation · quasi-probability stabilizer simulation · adaptive empirical variance estimation · extended stabilizer framework

Abstract

Classical simulability of quantum circuits plays a central role in characterizing and quantifying quantum computational advantage. Typically, the presence of non-Clifford gates introduces an exponential runtime overhead for classically estimating expectation values of observables. In this work, we introduce an efficient simulation framework that integrates the sum-over-Clifford method with quasi-probability-based stabilizer simulation to directly estimate expectation values. To optimize efficiency, we incorporate a circuit-adaptive reduction via variance estimation protocol, which terminates simulations once an empirical confidence bound is sufficient to guarantee the prescribed error tolerance. Our method circumvents overly conservative Hoeffding's inequality, thereby reducing the dependence on the gate-wise stabilizer extent from quadratic to linear in the low-variance regime, while maintaining the same space complexity as previous approaches. We explicitly prove the sample-complexity reduction for random quantum circuits and T-doped Clifford circuits and also empirically validate these advantages in the quantum approximate optimization algorithm and quantum kernel method.

item.arxave:abstract: Classical simulability of quantum circuits plays a central role in characterizing and quantifying quantum computational advantage. Typically, the presence of non-Clifford gates introduces an exponential runtime overhead for classically estimating expectation values of observables. In this work, we introduce an efficient simulation framework that integrates the sum-over-Clifford method with quasi-probability-based stabilizer simulation to directly estimate expectation values. To optimize efficiency, we incorporate a circuit-adaptive reduction via variance estimation protocol, which terminates simulations once an empirical confidence bound is sufficient to guarantee the prescribed error tolerance. Our method circumvents overly conservative Hoeffding's inequality, thereby reducing the dependence on the gate-wise stabilizer extent from quadratic to linear in the low-variance regime, while maintaining the same space complexity as previous approaches. We explicitly prove the sample-complexity reduction for random quantum circuits and T-doped Clifford circuits and also empirically validate these advantages in the quantum approximate optimization algorithm and quantum kernel method.

item.title: Shot-based variational simulation of the toric code phase transition: Energy, global entanglement, and noise resilience
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Shot-based VQE with parameterized circuits detects the toric code magnetic-field transition via energy derivatives and conditional global entanglement ΔG, yielding hc≈0.395 on a 2×2 lattice. Under depolarizing and readout noise, hc decreases linearly with noise scaling factor s, extrapolating to zero at s≈16.2.

Grade 0.363 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Hayede Zarei, Mohammad Hossein Zarei

Figure

Critical magnetic field hc as a function of noise scaling factor s for 2×2 (1024 shots) and 3×3 (64 shots) lattices. Solid lines show linear fits in the weak-noise regime demonstrating linear suppression of hc before high noise obscures the transition.

Asks

Can parameterized variational circuits on small periodic lattices reliably detect the toric-code topological phase transition and its entanglement signatures under finite-shot sampling and hardware noise?

But

Simulations restricted to 2×2 (8-qubit) and 3×3 (18-qubit) lattices; shot budgets limited to 1024 and 64 shots respectively; linear noise scaling holds only for low-noise regime (s≤2.5).

Tools

Qiskit Aer QASM Simulator · Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) · Depolarizing and readout noise channels · Finite-size scaling

Abstract

We investigate the capability of variational quantum circuits in detecting a topological phase transition within the toric code model subjected to a uniform magnetic field. The detection is carried out via shot-based computations of both the ground state energy and the global entanglement. We begin by employing well-established renormalization techniques to construct a quantum circuit that accurately represents the pure toric code under periodic boundary condition. This circuit is subsequently parameterized to enable a shot-based variational simulation of the ground state in the presence of the magnetic field. Our results demonstrate that even for the minimal lattice sizes and a finite number of measurement shots, the ground state energy exhibits a distinct singularity at the transition point which can be reliably approximated through finite-size scaling analysis. Furthermore, we introduce a secondary variational circuit designed to compute the global entanglement of the generated ground state. We observe that both global entanglement and its conditional counterpart display the expected qualitative behavior at the transition point, consistent with the topological nature of the phase transition. To evaluate the practical viability of our variational approach on real quantum hardware, we systematically examine the detrimental effects of gate noise on the analysis. We find that the topological phase exhibits a notable robustness against noise, manifesting as a linear decrease in the transition point with increasing noise strength.
